questions.question: Who among the following was awarded the Sansad Ratna Award 2023 and represents the Indian National Congress in Lok Sabha from West Bengal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury**, a senior leader of the Indian National Congress, represents the **Baharampur constituency in West Bengal** in the Lok Sabha.
 
• He was awarded the **Sansad Ratna Award 2023**, which recognizes outstanding parliamentarians for their exemplary performance in legislative work.
 
• Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury has been a prominent figure in Indian politics, serving as the **Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha** for the INC.
 
• The Sansad Ratna Awards, instituted by Prime Point Foundation, focus on evaluating MPs based on their work, such as debates, questions raised, private member bills, and attendance.
 
• Chowdhury's contributions in debates and discussions on critical issues earned him this prestigious recognition in 2023.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sansad Ratna Awards**

 
 
• These awards were introduced in 2010 and are based on data from the Indian Parliament's performance records.
 
• The awards aim to motivate parliamentarians to perform their legislative duties effectively.
 
• Only sitting MPs from the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are eligible for these awards.
 
• The selection process is conducted by an independent jury panel comprising senior parliamentarians and experts.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**
 
 
• Founded in 1885, it is one of the oldest political parties in India.
 
• The INC played a pivotal role in India's struggle for independence and was led by iconic leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.
 
• Post-independence, the INC has governed India for several decades and continues to be a major political party.
 
 
 
• **Lok Sabha**
 
 
• It is the lower house of the Indian Parliament, consisting of representatives directly elected by the people.
 
• The Lok Sabha is responsible for legislative functions, including law-making and budget approvals.
 
• Members of the Lok Sabha are elected for a term of five years.
 
 
 
• **Leader of Opposition**
 
 
• The Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha is the principal spokesperson of the opposition parties.
 
• They play a critical role in upholding the democratic process by challenging and scrutinizing the policies of the ruling government.
 
• The position is officially recognized if the opposition party has at least 10% of the total seats in Lok Sabha.

questions.question: Where is the Kala Ghoda Arts Festival organised every year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mumbai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Kala Ghoda Arts Festival** is an annual cultural festival held in the Kala Ghoda area of South Mumbai, Maharashtra.
 
• The festival was first started in **1999** and has since grown to become one of the most iconic art and cultural events in India.
 
• Organized by the **Kala Ghoda Association**, the event aims to preserve and promote art and heritage in the region.
 
• The festival spans nine days in early February each year, showcasing art, music, dance, theatre, literature, workshops, and culinary delights.
 
• It is a free-to-attend event, attracting thousands of visitors from across India and the world, making it a hub for cultural exchange and creativity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kala Ghoda:**

 
 
• Named after the iconic black horse (Kala Ghoda in Hindi) statue that once stood in the area.
 
• The Kala Ghoda precinct is known for its heritage buildings and vibrant cultural atmosphere.
 
 
 
• **The Festival's Offerings:**
 
 
• Covers diverse categories such as visual arts, cinema, theatre, literature, and architecture.
 
• Includes activities for children, heritage walks, and eco-friendly initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Impact on the Community:**
 
 
• Proceeds from the festival are used by the Kala Ghoda Association for the restoration of heritage buildings and public spaces.
 
• It serves as a platform for budding artists and performers to showcase their talent on an international stage.
 
 
 
• **Tourism and Economy:**
 
 
• The festival boosts tourism in Mumbai, drawing art enthusiasts, tourists, and locals alike.
 
• Contributes to the local economy through increased footfall in nearby businesses and markets.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel 'Amrit Aur Vish'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amritlal Nagar**__.

*__Key Points__

__
 
• **Amrit Aur Vish** is a critically acclaimed novel written by **Amritlal Nagar**, one of the most prominent Hindi novelists of the 20th century.
 
• The novel explores **social and moral dilemmas** through a historical and philosophical narrative.
 
• Amritlal Nagar is renowned for his ability to blend **historical and cultural themes** with contemporary societal issues.
 
• His literary works often focus on **human emotions, struggles, and societal dynamics**, making him a key figure in Hindi literature.
 
• Amritlal Nagar was awarded the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in 1967 for his novel Amrit Aur Vish*.

***Additional Information__**

 
• **Amritlal Nagar**

 
 
• Born on August 17, 1916, in Agra, he is considered one of the foundational figures of modern Hindi literature.
 
• He worked as a journalist and playwright before dedicating himself to writing novels and short stories.
 
• His famous works include Boond Aur Samudra*, *Manas Ka Hans*, and *Amrit Aur Vish*.
 
• He was honored with several awards, including the **Padma Bhushan** in 1969 for his contributions to Hindi literature.
 
 
 
• **Hindi Literature**
 
 
• Hindi literature has evolved over centuries, spanning **medieval, pre-modern, and modern periods**.
 
• Notable authors like Premchand, Harivansh Rai Bachchan, and Amritlal Nagar have enriched its legacy.
 
• It includes diverse forms such as poetry, novels, plays, and essays.
 
• Contemporary Hindi literature often addresses **social, political, and cultural themes**.
 
 
 
• **Sahitya Akademi Award**
 
 
• The Sahitya Akademi Award is a prestigious literary honor in India, established in 1954.
 
• It recognizes outstanding works in **24 Indian languages**, including Hindi.
 
• Authors like Amritlal Nagar, Premchand, and Mahadevi Varma have been recipients of this award.
 
• The award contributes to the promotion and preservation of Indian literature.
 
 
 
• **Historical Fiction in Hindi Literature**
 
 
• Historical fiction blends **historical events and settings with fictional storytelling**.
 
• Works like *Amrit Aur Vish* delve into India’s cultural and philosophical history.
 
• Such novels often reflect on **societal transformation and human values**.
 
• Amritlal Nagar’s contributions in this genre are widely regarded as timeless classics.

questions.question: Who inaugurated 'Vibrant Village Program' in April 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amit Shah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Union Home Minister **Amit Shah** inaugurated the 'Vibrant Village Program' on **10th April 2023**.
 
• The program was launched at Kibithoo, a border village in the **Anjaw district of Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
• Vibrant Village Program focuses on **developing infrastructure, livelihood opportunities, and essential amenities** for villages along India's northern borders.
 
• This initiative aims to **counter migration from border areas** and ensure sustainable development while boosting national security.
 
• The program specifically targets villages in states such as Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Ladakh.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Border Area Development Program (BADP):**

 
 
• BADP is an older initiative by the Indian government to **develop border areas** through infrastructure improvement and community welfare.
 
• It covers villages located within 10 kilometers of the international border in 16 states.
 
• BADP has been instrumental in addressing socio-economic challenges in border regions.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Border Villages:**
 
 
• Border villages play a critical role in **maintaining national security** and sovereignty.
 
• Development in border areas helps prevent **out-migration** and sustains local populations.
 
• Improved infrastructure enhances **connectivity and accessibility** for defense and civilian purposes.
 
 
 
• **India-China Border Dynamics:**
 
 
• India shares a **3,488-kilometer-long border** with China, spanning multiple states.
 
• Strengthening border infrastructure is crucial in light of ongoing **geopolitical tensions** with China.
 
• Programs like Vibrant Village help establish **strong local presence** in border areas.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Ministry of Home Affairs:**
 
 
• The Vibrant Village Program is spearheaded by the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is responsible for **internal security and border management**.
 
• The ministry coordinates with state governments and defense forces to implement development projects effectively.

questions.question: The 'Dhansiri' and 'Subansiri' are the tributaries of _______ River.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Dhansiri** and **Subansiri** are major tributaries of the **Brahmaputra River**, which flows through northeastern India.
 
• The Subansiri is the largest tributary of the Brahmaputra, originating in the **Tibet Autonomous Region of China** and entering India through Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• The Dhansiri River originates from **Laisang peak in Nagaland** and flows through Assam before meeting the Brahmaputra.
 
• The Brahmaputra is one of the major rivers in Asia, flowing through **Tibet, India, and Bangladesh**, and is known as the **Yarlung Tsangpo** in Tibet and **Jamuna** in Bangladesh.
 
• The Brahmaputra plays a crucial role in agriculture, hydropower, and transportation in the northeastern region of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmaputra River System:**

 
 
• The Brahmaputra is a transboundary river with a total length of about **2,900 km**.
 
• It is known for its strong current and frequent floods, particularly in the Assam Valley during the monsoon season.
 
• The river forms the world’s largest riverine island, **Majuli**, located in Assam.
 
 
 
• **Subansiri River:**
 
 
• Known as the "Gold River," it is renowned for its rich natural resources and hydropower potential.
 
• The Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project, one of India’s largest hydropower projects, is located on this river.
 
 
 
• **Dhansiri River:**
 
 
• The Dhansiri is vital for irrigation and serves as a lifeline for the agricultural communities in Nagaland and Assam.
 
• It is also a popular site for fishing and biodiversity conservation.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Brahmaputra:**
 
 
• The Brahmaputra Basin supports agriculture, fisheries, and livelihoods for millions of people in northeastern India and Bangladesh.
 
• The river is a critical source of freshwater and is essential for maintaining the ecosystem of the region.

questions.question: Why are wealth taxes and gift taxes treated as paper taxes in India?

options.text: It is not mandatory for the government to collect these taxes.
They do not generate much revenue in comparison to others.
Tax payers need to fill out forms only in paper and submit returns.
They are paid only by government employees, members of the Parliament and Legislative assemblies.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They do not generate much revenue in comparison to others**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Wealth taxes and gift taxes are considered "paper taxes" due to their **negligible contribution to overall tax revenue**.
 
• The administrative cost of collecting these taxes often **exceeds the revenue generated**, making them less economically viable.
 
• In India, the **Wealth Tax Act, 1957**, was abolished in 2015, emphasizing its limited utility as a revenue generator.
 
• Gift taxes were similarly repealed in 1998 but were later incorporated under the Income Tax Act, 1961, with restricted applicability, further reducing their impact on revenue.
 
• These taxes are primarily symbolic and have limited practical enforcement, leading to their classification as "paper taxes."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Wealth Tax Act, 1957:**

 
 
• Introduced to impose a tax on an individual's net wealth exceeding a certain threshold.
 
• Abolished in 2015 due to its **low revenue yield** and high compliance costs.
 
• Replaced by an additional surcharge on the super-rich as part of direct taxes.
 
 
 
• **Gift Tax Act, 1958:**
 
 
• Initially imposed a tax on monetary or property gifts exceeding a certain value.
 
• Repealed in 1998 and later brought under the Income Tax Act, 1961, with specific provisions for taxing gifts received above ₹50,000.
 
 
 
• **Income Tax Act, 1961:**
 
 
• Gifts above ₹50,000 are taxable under "Income from Other Sources" unless received from relatives or on special occasions like marriage.
 
• Gift tax provisions are limited to ensure simplicity and reduce administrative burden.
 
 
 
• **Economic Rationale:**
 
 
• Wealth and gift taxes are challenging to implement effectively due to **evasion and valuation complexities**.
 
• Countries with high compliance costs often shift to alternative taxation mechanisms to improve efficiency.

questions.question: What is the primary role of autotrophic organisms in an ecosystem?

options.text: Producing organic matter from inorganic substances
Preying on other organisms for food

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Producing organic matter from inorganic substances**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Autotrophic organisms**, such as plants, algae, and certain bacteria, are producers in an ecosystem.
 
• They utilize **photosynthesis or chemosynthesis** to convert inorganic substances (e.g., carbon dioxide and water) into organic matter.
 
• By producing organic compounds, autotrophs form the base of the food chain and provide energy to other organisms in the ecosystem.
 
• Photosynthetic autotrophs harness **solar energy**, while chemosynthetic autotrophs use chemical energy from inorganic molecules.
 
• Autotrophs play a vital role in maintaining **carbon balance** and oxygen levels in the environment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Photosynthesis:** A process where autotrophs convert sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and oxygen. It occurs in chloroplasts containing chlorophyll.
 
• **Chemosynthesis:** A process used by certain bacteria and archaea to produce organic matter using energy derived from chemical reactions, often in environments devoid of sunlight.
 
• **Trophic Levels:** Autotrophs belong to the **primary producer** level, forming the foundation of the food web.
 
• **Energy Flow:** The energy captured by autotrophs is transferred to consumers through feeding relationships, sustaining various life forms.
 
• **Carbon Fixation:** Autotrophs play a key role in the **carbon cycle** by converting atmospheric carbon dioxide into organic compounds, reducing greenhouse gases.

questions.question: Which of the following water bodies are also known as nurseries of the ocean?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Estuaries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Estuaries** are transition zones where freshwater from rivers meets and mixes with saltwater from the ocean, creating a unique ecological environment.
 
• They are often referred to as **"nurseries of the ocean"** because they provide critical breeding and feeding grounds for many marine species.
 
• Estuaries support a rich biodiversity, including fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and migratory birds, which thrive in their nutrient-rich waters.
 
• These areas are particularly important for the early life stages of commercially important fish species, such as salmon and shrimp.
 
• Estuaries play a vital role in maintaining water quality by filtering pollutants and sediments through their complex ecosystems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Definition of Estuaries:**

 
 
• An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of water where freshwater from rivers and streams merges with saltwater from the sea.
 
• They typically have a dynamic salinity gradient, influenced by tides, river flow, and seasonal changes.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Estuaries:**
 
 
• Estuaries act as natural buffers, protecting coastlines from erosion and flooding.
 
• They are crucial for nutrient cycling and support primary productivity, forming the foundation of aquatic food webs.
 
 
 
• **Threats to Estuaries:**
 
 
• Human activities such as pollution, overfishing, and land reclamation pose significant threats to estuarine ecosystems.
 
• Climate change impacts, including rising sea levels and altered precipitation patterns, further endanger these vital habitats.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Estuaries and Lagoons:**
 
 
• While estuaries are transition zones mixing freshwater and saltwater, lagoons are shallow coastal water bodies separated from the ocean by sandbars or barrier islands.
 
• Lagoons typically have less biodiversity compared to estuaries due to limited nutrient mixing.

questions.question: Identify the Kuchipudi dancer, actor and film producer who won the best choreography award at the 68th National Film Awards 2022.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sandhya Raju**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Sandhya Raju is a renowned **Kuchipudi dancer**, actor, and film producer from India.
 
• She won the **Best Choreography Award** at the **68th National Film Awards 2022** for her work in the film "**Natyam**".
 
• **Natyam**, a Telugu-language film, highlights the importance of classical dance and was both choreographed and acted by Sandhya Raju.
 
• Her choreography in Natyam showcased intricate Kuchipudi techniques, earning her national recognition.
 
• Sandhya Raju is also known for her efforts to revive and promote **Kuchipudi**, one of India's classical dance forms, through her performances and cinematic ventures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kuchipudi Dance:**

 
 
• Kuchipudi is one of the eight classical dance forms of India, originating from the village of Kuchipudi in Andhra Pradesh.
 
• It is known for its **graceful movements, expressive gestures, and dramatic storytelling**.
 
• Traditionally, Kuchipudi was performed as dance dramas based on themes from Hindu mythology, particularly the epics Mahabharata and Ramayana.
 
• It combines elements of **nritta (pure dance), nritya (expressive dance), and natya (dramatic art)**.
 
 
 
• **National Film Awards:**
 
 
• The National Film Awards are one of the most prestigious film awards in India, established in 1954.
 
• They are presented annually by the Directorate of Film Festivals, under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
 
• The awards aim to honor artistic, technical, and social contributions to Indian cinema.
 
 
 
• **Sandhya Raju's Background:**
 
 
• Sandhya Raju is a disciple of **Guru Vempati Chinna Satyam**, a legendary Kuchipudi maestro.
 
• She has performed extensively both in India and internationally, showcasing the rich heritage of Kuchipudi.
 
 
 
• **68th National Film Awards (2022):**
 
 
• The 68th National Film Awards recognized films from the year 2020, delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
 
• It included various categories like Best Feature Film, Best Actor, Best Actress, and Best Choreography, among others.

questions.question: Tanras Khan is associated with which of the following gharanas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Delhi gharana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Tanras Khan was a prominent figure associated with the **Delhi Gharana** of Hindustani classical music.
 
• He was known for his expertise in **tabla** and for establishing a systematic approach to tabla compositions.
 
• The Delhi Gharana is considered the oldest tabla gharana, with a focus on clarity, precision, and intricate rhythmic structures.
 
• Tanras Khan was instrumental in shaping the rhythmic patterns (kaidas and tukras) of the Delhi Gharana, which are still widely practiced today.
 
• The gharana's influence extends beyond tabla to vocal and instrumental music, reflecting a holistic approach to rhythm and melody.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Delhi Gharana:**

 
 
• One of the oldest tabla gharanas, established in the 18th century.
 
• It emphasizes a balance of tonal clarity and rhythmic complexity in its compositions.
 
• Key contributions include kaidas, tukras, and parans that are foundational to modern tabla playing.
 
 
 
• **Tabla Gharanas:**
 
 
• There are six prominent tabla gharanas: Delhi, Lucknow, Benaras, Ajrada, Farrukhabad, and Punjab.
 
• Each gharana has a distinct style of playing, composition, and teaching.
 
 
 
• **Role of Gharanas in Hindustani Classical Music:**
 
 
• Gharanas represent a lineage or school of music with distinct styles and techniques.
 
• They preserve and pass down traditional knowledge and innovations in music and dance.
 
 
 
• **Tanras Khan's Legacy:**
 
 
• His contributions to the Delhi Gharana have made it a cornerstone of tabla tradition.
 
• He played a pivotal role in standardizing tabla compositions, ensuring their survival and transmission over generations.

questions.question: According to the standard definition of Census of India, the marginal worker is a person who works for less than _______ days in a year.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**183**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the Census of India, a **marginal worker** is defined as a person who worked for less than 183 days in a year.
 
• Marginal workers are distinguished from **main workers**, who work for 183 days or more annually.
 
• Marginal workers contribute to economic activities on a part-time basis or during specific seasons.
 
• The classification of workers into marginal and main categories helps in assessing the degree of employment stability and dependency in the workforce.
 
• This categorization is crucial for understanding labor market dynamics and designing targeted policies for employment generation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Census of India**

 
 
• Conducted every 10 years, the Census is the largest single source of statistical data on population, workforce, and socio-economic parameters in India.
 
• The Census categorizes workers into main workers, marginal workers, and non-workers.
 
• The latest Census was conducted in 2011, and the next is expected in the near future.
 
 
 
• **Workforce Classification**
 
 
• Workers are classified as **cultivators, agricultural laborers, household industry workers,** and **other workers** based on their primary occupation.
 
• Marginal workers are often engaged in seasonal agricultural activities or casual labor.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Marginal Workers**
 
 
• Marginal workers play a crucial role in sectors requiring temporary or seasonal labor, such as agriculture and construction.
 
• Their participation highlights the prevalence of underemployment and dependency on informal sectors.
 
 
 
• **Employment Challenges**
 
 
• The presence of marginal workers indicates challenges in ensuring **stable employment opportunities** for the population.
 
• Government schemes such as MGNREGA aim to address these challenges by providing 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to rural households.

questions.question: The Banaras session of the Indian National Congress in 1905 was presided over by ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gopal Krishna Gokhale**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Banaras session of the Indian National Congress in 1905 was presided over by **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**, a prominent leader and social reformer.
 
• Gokhale was a key advocate of **moderate politics** within the Congress, focusing on constitutional reforms and dialogue with British authorities.
 
• The Banaras session marked a pivotal moment as it addressed the **Partition of Bengal (1905)**, which created widespread unrest in India.
 
• Under Gokhale’s leadership, the Congress strongly condemned the partition and emphasized the need for **Swadeshi (self-reliance) and boycott of British goods**.
 
• Gokhale's vision during the session laid the foundation for future strategies in India's freedom movement, blending moderation with a growing emphasis on self-reliance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Partition of Bengal (1905):**

 
 
• It was carried out by Lord Curzon, the then Viceroy of India, citing administrative convenience as the reason.
 
• The partition divided Bengal into East Bengal (Muslim-majority) and West Bengal (Hindu-majority), which led to widespread protests.
 
• The move was seen as an attempt to divide and rule by creating communal divisions.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• Launched as a response to the Partition of Bengal, it urged Indians to boycott British goods and promote indigenous products.
 
• The movement also emphasized self-reliance in education, industries, and governance.
 
 
 
• **Role of Gopal Krishna Gokhale:**
 
 
• Gokhale was a disciple of social reformer Mahadev Govind Ranade and a mentor to Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• He founded the **Servants of India Society** in 1905 to promote education and social reforms.
 
 
 
• **Moderates vs. Extremists in INC:**
 
 
• The early 1900s saw a growing rift in the Congress between Moderates (like Gokhale) and Extremists (like Bal Gangadhar Tilak).
 
• Moderates advocated dialogue and reforms, while Extremists demanded direct action and self-rule.

questions.question: The 'Agaria' community of the 19th century was associated with which of the following industries?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron industry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Agaria community of the 19th century was primarily engaged in the **iron smelting industry**, producing iron from locally sourced ore.
 
• This community belonged to the **tribal regions of central India**, particularly in areas such as Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.
 
• The Agarias were known for their traditional techniques of iron smelting, which involved using **indigenous furnaces and charcoal**.
 
• Their expertise in iron production was significant for creating tools, weapons, and agricultural implements used in local economies.
 
• Colonial policies and the advent of modern industrial iron production led to the decline of the Agaria's traditional iron industry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indigenous iron smelting:** Traditional iron smelting involved using small clay furnaces and charcoal as fuel. The process relied on local knowledge passed down through generations.
 
• **Impact of British policies:** During colonial rule, the British discouraged traditional industries like iron smelting by imposing heavy taxes and promoting imported iron and steel.
 
• **Charcoal usage:** The Agarias used charcoal derived from local forests as a primary fuel for their furnaces, making their practices sustainable but labor-intensive.
 
• **Decline of traditional practices:** The introduction of modern iron-making technologies, such as blast furnaces, rendered traditional methods economically unviable, leading to the marginalization of communities like the Agarias.
 
• **Cultural significance:** The Agaria community's craft was deeply integrated into their social and cultural identity, symbolizing their connection to the land and natural resources.

questions.question: Pushyamitra Sunga's capital was at:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pataliputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Pushyamitra Sunga, the founder of the Sunga Dynasty, established his capital at **Pataliputra**, which was a significant political and cultural hub in ancient India.
 
• Pataliputra (modern-day Patna) was strategically located near the confluence of the Ganga, Son, and Gandak rivers, making it a center of trade and administration.
 
• Pushyamitra Sunga overthrew the Mauryan Empire in 185 BCE and assumed control, marking a shift in political power.
 
• The city of Pataliputra continued to remain an important administrative center under the Sunga Dynasty.
 
• The Sunga rulers were known for their promotion of Hinduism and revival of Vedic traditions, which flourished in Pataliputra during their reign.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sunga Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Sunga Dynasty was established by Pushyamitra Sunga after the decline of the Mauryan Empire.
 
• It lasted for approximately 112 years, from 185 BCE to 73 BCE.
 
• The dynasty is known for its contributions to Indian art, architecture, and culture, particularly in the development of the Shunga art style.
 
 
 
• **Pataliputra:**
 
 
• Pataliputra was originally founded by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru in the 5th century BCE.
 
• It served as the capital for several major dynasties, including the Nandas, Mauryas, Sungas, and Guptas.
 
• The city was an ancient center of learning and housed scholars, including those from Nalanda and Taxila.
 
 
 
• **Pushyamitra Sunga:**
 
 
• He was a Brahmin military general under the Mauryan Emperor Brihadratha before he assassinated him to establish the Sunga Dynasty.
 
• Pushyamitra is known for conducting Ashvamedha Yajnas (horse sacrifices) to assert his authority and revive Vedic practices.
 
• His reign marked the decline of Buddhism and the resurgence of Hinduism in the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Pataliputra:**
 
 
• The city played a crucial role in shaping the political, economic, and cultural history of ancient India.
 
• Its strategic location made it a key center for trade, administration, and military activities.
 
• Pataliputra also witnessed the construction of several architectural marvels, including wooden structures and fortifications.

questions.question: What is the charge of an electron?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Negative**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An electron carries a **negative electrical charge**, which is equal to -1 elementary charge (approximately -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs).
 
• Electrons are one of the three main subatomic particles, along with protons and neutrons, that make up an atom.
 
• The negative charge of an electron balances the positive charge of a proton in a neutral atom.
 
• Electrons are extremely small in mass, approximately 1/1836 of the mass of a proton or neutron.
 
• In an atom, electrons are found in regions called **electron clouds** or orbitals, surrounding the nucleus.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Elementary Charge:**

 
 
• The charge of an electron is referred to as the **elementary charge**, denoted as "e," which is approximately -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs.
 
• It is the smallest unit of electric charge that is considered indivisible in nature.
 
 
 
• **Subatomic Particles:**
 
 
• Atoms consist of three primary subatomic particles: electrons (negative charge), protons (positive charge), and neutrons (neutral charge).
 
• The number of protons and electrons in a neutral atom is equal, resulting in no net charge.
 
 
 
• **Atomic Structure:**
 
 
• Electrons orbit the nucleus of an atom in defined energy levels or shells, governed by quantum mechanics.
 
• The specific arrangement of electrons determines the chemical properties of an element.
 
 
 
• **Discovery of the Electron:**
 
 
• The electron was discovered by **J.J. Thomson** in 1897 through his cathode ray tube experiment.
 
• This discovery led to the development of the "plum pudding model" of the atom, which was later revised by the nuclear model proposed by Rutherford.
 
 
 
• **Role in Electricity:**
 
 
• Electrons are responsible for the flow of electric current in conductive materials.
 
• This movement of electrons under the influence of an electric field forms the basis of electricity.

questions.question: Excessive bleeding from wounds may happen due to lack of ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vitamin K**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Vitamin K** is an essential nutrient required for blood clotting (coagulation) and preventing excessive bleeding from wounds.
 
• It helps in the synthesis of proteins such as **prothrombin**, which are crucial for the blood clotting process.
 
• A deficiency in Vitamin K can result in **impaired clotting**, leading to prolonged bleeding and easy bruising.
 
• Newborns are particularly at risk of Vitamin K deficiency, which is why they are often given Vitamin K injections at birth to prevent **Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB)**.
 
• Vitamin K is found in green leafy vegetables like spinach, kale, and broccoli, as well as in smaller amounts in dairy products, meat, and eggs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Vitamin K:**

 
 
• **Vitamin K1 (Phylloquinone):** Found primarily in plant-based foods such as green leafy vegetables.
 
• **Vitamin K2 (Menaquinone):** Found in fermented foods and animal products and also produced by gut bacteria.
 
 
 
• **Role in Bone Health:** Vitamin K also plays a role in bone metabolism by helping to regulate calcium levels in the body and supporting bone mineralization.
 
• **Symptoms of Deficiency:** In addition to excessive bleeding, Vitamin K deficiency may cause symptoms like blood in stool or urine, nosebleeds, and heavy menstrual bleeding.
 
• **Vitamin K Antagonists:** Drugs like warfarin act as Vitamin K antagonists and are used to prevent blood clots in conditions such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and atrial fibrillation.
 
• **Daily Requirement:** The recommended daily intake of Vitamin K varies by age and gender, with adult males requiring approximately 120 micrograms and adult females requiring about 90 micrograms per day.

questions.question: What is the term for a dome-shaped monument that contains sacred relics in Buddhism?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stupa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **Stupa** is a dome-shaped architectural structure that serves as a sacred monument in Buddhism, often housing relics of the Buddha or other significant monks.
 
• It symbolizes the **enlightened mind** and the path to enlightenment in Buddhist philosophy.
 
• Stupas are typically surrounded by a **circumambulatory path** where devotees walk in a clockwise direction as an act of devotion.
 
• Some of the most famous stupas include the **Sanchi Stupa** in India, the Great Stupa at Borobudur in Indonesia, and the Boudhanath Stupa in Nepal.
 
• Stupas are often adorned with **ornamental gateways (toranas)** and inscriptions that depict Buddhist teachings and historical events.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vihar**: Refers to a Buddhist monastery or residence for monks and nuns, often used as a place for meditation and learning.
 
• **Chaitya**: A prayer hall or shrine in Buddhism, often containing a stupa and used for congregational worship.
 
• **Stambha**: A free-standing pillar, often inscribed with edicts or symbols of Buddhist philosophy, such as the Ashokan Pillars.
 
• **Relics in Stupas**: These may include physical remains of the Buddha, such as ashes or bones, as well as objects associated with him, like sacred texts or robes.
 
• **Symbolism of the Stupa**: The dome represents the universe, the square base symbolizes the earth, and the spire signifies spiritual ascent or enlightenment.

questions.question: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court of India propound the Basic Structure Doctrine of the Constitution?

options.text: Kesavanand Bharti vs. State of Kerala Case
Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India Case
Golaknath vs. State of Punjab Case
Indira Gandhi vs. Raj Narayan Case

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala Case**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala** case (1973) is a landmark judgment by the Supreme Court of India where the **Basic Structure Doctrine** was propounded.
 
• This doctrine asserts that **certain fundamental features of the Constitution cannot be amended by the Parliament**.
 
• The case arose when Kesavananda Bharati, a religious leader, challenged the Kerala government’s attempts to impose restrictions on his property under land reform laws.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled by a narrow majority of 7:6 that while Parliament has wide powers to amend the Constitution under Article 368, it **cannot alter its basic structure**.
 
• This doctrine ensures that the core principles of the Constitution, such as **democracy, secularism, federalism, and the rule of law**, remain intact.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:**

 
 
• It is a judicial principle that limits the amending power of Parliament to ensure the Constitution's basic features are preserved.
 
• Examples of basic structure elements include the supremacy of the Constitution, independence of the judiciary, and the secular character of the state.
 
 
 
• **Article 368:**
 
 
• It deals with the powers and procedure of Parliament to amend the Constitution.
 
• The Kesavananda Bharati case clarified that this power is not absolute and is subject to judicial review.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review:**
 
 
• The power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative acts and executive orders.
 
• The Basic Structure Doctrine strengthens judicial review as a safeguard against unconstitutional amendments.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Cases:**
 
 
• **Golaknath vs. State of Punjab (1967):** Held that fundamental rights cannot be amended under Article 368.
 
• **Indira Gandhi vs. Raj Narayan (1975):** Applied the Basic Structure Doctrine to strike down the 39th Amendment.
 
• **Minerva Mills vs. Union of India (1980):** Reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine, emphasizing the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles.

questions.question: Anahat Singh is associated with which of the following sports events?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Squash**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Anahat Singh** is a young and talented squash player from India, known for her exceptional performance at the junior level.
 
• She gained prominence by winning the **U-11, U-13, and U-15 titles** at various international squash tournaments.
 
• Anahat represented India in the **Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games** at just 14 years of age, making her the youngest participant in squash at the event.
 
• She has achieved significant success, including a title at the prestigious **British Junior Open Squash** tournament.
 
• Anahat Singh is regarded as a rising star in Indian squash, showcasing immense potential to excel on the global stage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Squash:**

 
 
• Squash is a racquet sport played by two players (singles) or four players (doubles) in a four-walled court.
 
• The game involves hitting a small, hollow rubber ball against the walls of the court.
 
• It requires agility, precision, and tactical thinking, making it a physically demanding sport.
 
• Squash has been recognized by the **World Squash Federation (WSF)**, which governs international competitions.
 
 
 
• **British Junior Open Squash:**
 
 
• The British Junior Open is one of the most prestigious junior squash tournaments in the world.
 
• It attracts top junior players globally and serves as a platform for young talent to showcase their skills.
 
• Anahat Singh’s victory at this tournament highlights her skill and potential in squash.
 
 
 
• **Commonwealth Games:**
 
 
• The Commonwealth Games is a multi-sport event involving athletes from the Commonwealth of Nations.
 
• Squash has been a part of the Commonwealth Games since 1998, offering a platform for global competition.
 
• Anahat Singh’s participation in the 2022 Games marked a milestone for Indian squash.
 
 
 
• **India's Rising Stars in Squash:**
 
 
• India has seen a growth in squash popularity due to players like **Dipika Pallikal**, **Saurav Ghosal**, and **Joshna Chinappa**.
 
• Anahat Singh is considered part of the next generation of Indian squash players aiming to achieve international acclaim.

questions.question: Fugdi is famous dance of the state of ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Goa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Fugdi** is a traditional folk dance of Goa, performed primarily by women during festivals and special occasions.
 
• The dance is usually performed in **circles or rows**, accompanied by rhythmic clapping and singing.
 
• Fugdi is often showcased during the Hindu festivals of **Ganesh Chaturthi** and other celebrations, symbolizing joy and unity.
 
• This dance form is particularly popular among **Konkani-speaking communities** of Goa.
 
• Fugdi is characterized by its **energetic movements** and simple yet vibrant choreography, reflecting the cultural essence of Goa.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Goan Folk Culture:**

 
 
• Goa is renowned for its rich cultural heritage, blending Portuguese influences with traditional Indian art forms.
 
• Along with Fugdi, other popular folk dances of Goa include **Dekhni, Dhalo, and Mando**.
 
• Music and dance play a vital role in Goan festivals, showcasing the vibrant spirit of the region.
 
 
 
• **Konkani Language and Art:**
 
 
• Konkani is the official language of Goa, deeply intertwined with its folk traditions and performing arts.
 
• Goan art forms often depict themes from daily life, local legends, and devotion to deities.
 
 
 
• **Ganesh Chaturthi:**
 
 
• Ganesh Chaturthi is one of the most celebrated festivals in Goa, dedicated to Lord Ganesha.
 
• During this festival, Fugdi is performed by women as an expression of devotion and happiness.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Folk Dances:**
 
 
• Folk dances like Fugdi serve as a medium to preserve and promote regional traditions.
 
• They reflect the social, religious, and cultural fabric of the community.

questions.question: The Border-Gavaskar trophy is played between ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**India and Australia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Border-Gavaskar Trophy** is a Test cricket series played between **India and Australia**.
 
• The trophy is named after two cricketing legends, **Allan Border** of Australia and **Sunil Gavaskar** of India.
 
• It was first contested during the **1996/97 cricket season** when India hosted Australia for a one-off Test match.
 
• The Border-Gavaskar Trophy is a **bilateral Test series**, and its matches are part of the **ICC World Test Championship** since its inception in 2019.
 
• India has dominated the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in recent years, including memorable series wins in Australia in **2018-19** and **2020-21**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Allan Border:**

 
 
• Allan Border is a former Australian cricketer who captained the Australian team for most of the 1980s.
 
• He is regarded as one of the greatest batsmen in cricket history and was the first player to reach **11,000 Test runs**.
 
 
 
• **Sunil Gavaskar:**
 
 
• Sunil Gavaskar is a former Indian cricketer and one of the finest opening batsmen in the history of cricket.
 
• He was the first player to score **10,000 Test runs** and held the record for most centuries in Test cricket (34) for many years.
 
 
 
• **Significant Matches:**
 
 
• The 2001 Kolkata Test (Eden Gardens) is one of the most iconic matches in the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, where India achieved a historic victory after following on.
 
• The 2020-21 series marked a remarkable comeback by India after being bowled out for **36 in Adelaide**, culminating in a series win at the Gabba, Brisbane.
 
 
 
• **ICC World Test Championship:**
 
 
• The Border-Gavaskar Trophy is now a part of the ICC World Test Championship, adding more significance to the series.
 
• The ICC World Test Championship aims to crown the best Test cricket team globally through a league format.

questions.question: Which of the following reports is considered as a piecemeal effort to provide resilience to the successful working of federal system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sarkaria Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sarkaria Commission was constituted in **1983** by the Government of India to review the working of the **Indian federal system** and suggest reforms for strengthening it.
 
• The Commission focused on recommending measures to ensure better coordination between the **Centre and the States**, addressing grievances of states while maintaining national unity.
 
• It emphasized the need for cooperative federalism and suggested several reforms to provide resilience to the federal system.
 
• Its recommendations covered various aspects, including **legislative relations, administrative relations, financial relations, and emergency provisions**.
 
• Many of its suggestions have been used as a reference point in debates and policies to ensure smooth functioning of the Centre-State relations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federal System in India**

 
 
• India follows a **quasi-federal system**, where the Constitution provides for a strong Centre along with state governments with defined powers.
 
• The distribution of powers is enumerated in the **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List** under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Important Recommendations of Sarkaria Commission**
 
 
• Strengthen the role of the Inter-State Council for resolving disputes between states and the Centre.
 
• Restrict the misuse of **Article 356 (President’s Rule)** and ensure its application only in exceptional circumstances.
 
• Encourage decentralization by empowering states and local bodies.
 
 
 
• **Other Commissions and Their Purposes**
 
 
• **Kothari Commission (1964-66):** Focused on reforms in the education system of India.
 
• **Thakkar Commission (1984):** Investigated the assassination of Indira Gandhi.
 
• **Kapur Commission:** Investigated the conspiracy behind the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
 
 
• **Inter-State Council**
 
 
• It is a constitutional body under **Article 263** of the Indian Constitution, aimed at resolving disputes and fostering cooperation between the Centre and States.
 
• It was set up based on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission in **1990**.

questions.question: In 1527, Babur defeated Rana Sanga, the Rajput ruler of Mewar in the Battle of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Khanwa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Battle of Khanwa was fought on **March 16, 1527**, between the Mughal Emperor Babur and Rana Sanga, the Rajput ruler of Mewar.
 
• Babur’s victory at Khanwa marked the **consolidation of Mughal power in India**, following his earlier victory in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
 
• Babur employed advanced military tactics, including the use of **field artillery**, which played a decisive role in securing his victory.
 
• The battle ended Rana Sanga’s aspirations of uniting Indian rulers to oppose the Mughal invasion, significantly weakening Rajput resistance.
 
• Khanwa is located in modern-day Rajasthan and is historically significant as one of the pivotal battles in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Babur’s Military Tactics**

 
 
• Babur introduced the **Ottoman-style Tulughma and Araba tactics** in Indian warfare, which involved splitting the army into smaller units for flexible maneuvers.
 
• He effectively used **gunpowder and artillery** in battles, which was relatively new in Indian warfare at the time.
 
 
 
• **Rana Sanga**
 
 
• Rana Sanga was a prominent Rajput ruler and is remembered for his efforts to resist foreign invasions and unite Indian rulers against Babur.
 
• Despite his defeat at Khanwa, Rana Sanga remains a symbol of Rajput valor and resistance.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Battle**
 
 
• The Battle of Khanwa solidified Babur’s position as the ruler of Northern India and laid the foundation for the Mughal Empire.
 
• It demonstrated the superiority of Babur’s military strategies and modern weaponry over traditional Indian warfare methods.
 
 
 
• **Baburnama**
 
 
• The Battle of Khanwa is vividly described in Babur’s autobiography, **Baburnama**, providing firsthand insight into his strategies and the significance of the victory.
 
• Baburnama remains one of the most important historical sources for the study of Mughal history.

questions.question: According to the Multidimensional Poverty Index 2023, which union territory has the least percentage of poor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Puducherry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) 2023, **Puducherry** has the least percentage of poor among Union Territories in India.
 
• The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures poverty across multiple dimensions, including health, education, and standard of living.
 
• Puducherry’s achievement is attributed to its strong focus on social welfare schemes and improved access to education and healthcare facilities.
 
• As per the MPI 2023 report, Puducherry exhibits minimal deprivation across indicators like child nutrition, school attendance, and access to basic amenities.
 
• Other Union Territories like Lakshadweep, Delhi, and Chandigarh also perform well but fall behind Puducherry in terms of the lowest poverty rate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**

 
 
• The MPI is a global measure of poverty developed by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).
 
• It assesses poverty using three dimensions: health, education, and standard of living, further divided into 10 indicators.
 
• An individual is considered multidimensionally poor if they are deprived in at least one-third of these weighted indicators.
 
 
 
• **Poverty Reduction in India**
 
 
• India has witnessed significant poverty reduction in recent years, driven by welfare programs, economic growth, and improved governance.
 
• Programs like Ayushman Bharat, National Food Security Act, and Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) have contributed to poverty alleviation.
 
 
 
• **Performance of Union Territories**
 
 
• Union Territories like Puducherry, Lakshadweep, and Chandigarh consistently perform well due to focused administration and smaller populations.
 
• Access to universal healthcare, education, and welfare initiatives plays a key role in reducing poverty in these regions.
 
 
 
• **India’s MPI Ranking**
 
 
• India's overall performance in the MPI 2023 reflects its commitment to achieving Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty.
 
• The MPI findings provide critical insights for policymakers to address regional disparities and target areas requiring urgent intervention.

questions.question: The North-South National Highway Corridor connects which two UTs/States of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jammu and Kashmir - Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The North-South National Highway Corridor is part of the **Golden Quadrilateral project**, which aims to connect India's four major geographical extents.
 
• The corridor spans from **Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir (North)** to **Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu (South)**.
 
• It is one of the four primary highway networks under the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) initiated by the Government of India.
 
• The North-South Corridor covers a distance of approximately **4,000 kilometers**, making it one of the longest highway stretches in India.
 
• This corridor significantly boosts connectivity, trade, and transportation between India's northernmost and southernmost regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) Project**

 
 
• The Golden Quadrilateral is a highway network connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata.
 
• It was launched in 1999 under the National Highways Development Project (NHDP).
 
• The project aims to enhance connectivity between India's major cities and industrial hubs.
 
 
 
• **National Highways Development Project (NHDP)**
 
 
• NHDP is a flagship program by the Government of India for upgrading, rehabilitating, and expanding the country's highway network.
 
• It includes the Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West Corridors, Port Connectivity, and other projects.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the North-South Corridor**
 
 
• It reduces travel time and transportation costs for goods and passengers.
 
• Facilitates economic integration by connecting agricultural, industrial, and urban centers across India.
 
• Boosts tourism by providing improved road access to key destinations.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Indian National Highways**
 
 
• National Highways constitute about 2% of India's road network but carry around 40% of total road traffic.
 
• They are managed by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
 
• India's highways include expressways, toll roads, and standard highways to ensure efficient connectivity.
